lines.text: Istanbul sits on two continents, split by the Bosphorus, a strait of water between Europe and Asia.
So how do you get a railway under the sea? Engineers did it in pieces.
The deepest point sits near sixty meters below the surface.
They only sank a section when the current ran under three knots.
First, they cast eleven concrete sections in dry docks. Each one weighs up to eighteen thousand tonnes.
Then they tested each section and towed it out to the strait.
Crews dredged a trench into the seabed, about fourteen meters deep.
The sections were lowered by filling internal tanks with water, slowly, under control.
Machines levelled a gravel bed, and grout filled the gaps underneath.
Each joint is sealed with rubber gaskets, and then the water is pumped out.
At each shore, the tube links to bored tunnels that run into the hills.
Joined end to end, the sections make a tube of about one thousand, three hundred eighty seven meters. Trains now cross under the water, from Europe to Asia.
